--- Page 1 ---
Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench:
The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
Xiaojun Wu∗1,2, Cehao Yang∗1,2, Xuhui Jiang1,3,
Chengjin Xu1,3, Jia Li† 2, Jian Guo† 1
1IDEA Research
2The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
3DataArcTech Ltd.
Abstract
Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended
real-world problem into assumptions, a model,
a solution, and a defended recommendation,
and its answers matter only if they are both
close to a credible reference and physically fea-
sible; existing benchmarks either score solver
fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge,
leaving those numbers unchecked. We intro-
duce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Math-
ematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark
to make complete contest-style modeling prob-
lems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once,
over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems
(2023–2025). Each task ships the verbatim
statement, official attachments, and figures in
a containerized terminal; the agent returns one
JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of
the final question against a reproduction of the
Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices
distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scor-
ing, which never penalises beating the anchor,
and two-layer feasibility verification—a pro-
grammatic gate over six decidable invariant
forms plus 624 Lean 4 obligations—with a
hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each
task is scored against a panel of human out-
standing papers rather than one, so a model
must be close to many accepted answers; across
seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the
strongest reach a multi-reference O-EVAL of
64.58%, while the $2.54 open model holds
59.81% at 1/100 the cost.
TB-MathModel
turns the numeric core of modeling into a repro-
ducible, machine-checkable signal for measur-
ing long-horizon modeling competence and for
collecting agent trajectories. The source code
is available at https://github.com/wxj630/
terminal-bench-math-modeling.
1
Introduction
Mathematical modeling contests such as CUMCM
in China and MCM/ICM internationally ask teams
*Equal Contribution
†Corresponding Author
to convert a deliberately under-specified real-world
problem into a defensible quantitative answer
within days. The deliverable is not a single num-
ber but a chain: assumptions →model →solution
→sensitivity →recommendation. Two properties
make it an attractive target for agent evaluation:
it is quantitative, because the final question ends
in numbers that can be checked, and it is multi-
modal, because statements reference figures and
attachments are spreadsheets and CSVs. It also
differs from solving a well-posed problem in where
the hard work begins—the model itself must be
built, and the same situation admits time-series,
optimization, dynamical, graph, or multi-criteria
formulations, any of which can be defensible if its
assumptions are explicit and its computation cred-
ible (Giordano et al., 2014; Meerschaert, 2013).
This is what makes modeling a demanding test of
long-horizon agents: hold the statement and at-
tachments in context, choose a formulation, write
and run code, handle files and units, and report a
self-consistent answer.
Existing benchmarks cover adjacent but distinct
ground, and none closes the loop we care about.
Code, terminal, and assistant benchmarks score
repository edits, command-line competence, and
tool use (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026;
Mialon et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025); closed-form
mathematics benchmarks score deduction rather
than modeling (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Cobbe et al.,
2021; Glazer et al., 2024); operations-research
datasets parse word problems into solver-ready
formulations (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; Ahma-
diTeshnizi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). The
closest prior work on modeling itself falls into two
camps, neither simultaneously agentic, verifiable,
terminal, and multimodal. One stays solver-facing
and narrow, scoring a single formal artifact (Huang
et al., 2025b). The other grades the final report with
an LLM judge (Qian et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025),
rewarding fluent prose without establishing that the
1
arXiv:2611.08237v1  [cs.CL]  5 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
reported numbers are correct or even admissible.
Table 1 makes the gap concrete; TB-MathModel is
the first to combine all of these properties.
Closing the gap raises three problems that shape
the design. Different teams make different assump-
tions, so there is no single ground truth: rather than
promote one paper to truth, TB-MathModel asks
every human expert, scoring each task against a
panel of outstanding solutions so that a model must
be close to many accepted answers, not match one.
Anchoring creates asymmetric failure—a model
that does better than the paper can score worse than
one that copies it—so TB-MathModel makes each
metric’s direction explicit and scores one-sidedly.
And a wrong-but-plausible answer is easy to pro-
duce (numbers that look reasonable yet violate the
problem’s physics), which anchor comparison can-
not catch, so TB-MathModel adds an independent
feasibility layer.
We present TB-MathModel (Terminal-style
Mathematical Modeling Bench), to our knowledge
the first benchmark to turn complete contest-style
mathematical modeling problems into an agentic,
verifiable, terminal evaluation. It contributes:
1. The first benchmark of its kind, and the 18-
task dataset behind it. No prior benchmark
turns complete contest-style modeling prob-
lems into a containerized terminal task with
an executable verifier. TB-MathModel cov-
ers CUMCM and MCM 2023–2025 (problems
A/B/C each year), with verbatim statements,
official attachments, 21 figures cropped from
the PDFs, and one JSON artifact per task.
2. Direction-aware, one-sided scoring with
auditable edge-case rules.
Per-metric se-
mantic directions (higher/lower_is_better,
target_value, exact_value); two reported
metrics (O-EVAL, ROBUST BO-EVAL); ex-
plicit rules for degenerate bands and unpinned
reference units; and contract tests that lock the
two defining properties down.
3. A two-layer feasibility verification design.
A programmatic gate covering 18/18 tasks
through six decidable invariant forms, and a
Lean 4 certificate layer of 624 kernel-checked
obligations; the two layers decide every feasi-
bility question a structured artifact can settle,
and state exactly where an independent replay
takes over.
4. An empirical study of seven multimodal
model/harness entries, each averaged over
three seeds, with per-task behaviour, a cost–
robustness analysis, and three case studies; we
also document the scoring pitfalls we found and
fixed and quantify which move the leaderboard.
Against the human panel, the two newest flag-
ships lead (GPT-6 Astra + codex at O-EVAL
64.58 ± 2.93 and MULTI-BO 1.132, Fable 5.1 +
claude-code at 63.11±1.33 and 1.081, means over
three seeds), while the $2.54 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
+ opencode holds 59.81 ± 1.25 at 1/100 the cost;
varying only the harness moves O-EVAL by at most
0.07 pp, so the board measures the model rather
than the harness. Per-seed deviations reach 2.9 pp,
so adjacent rows are not significantly separated.
One case study inverts the usual story: on dragon-
dance the models were right and our anchor was
wrong—the sharpest argument for independently
checkable feasibility.
2
Related Work
Agent and assistant benchmarks.
Software-
engineering and terminal agents are measured
by repository-level tasks (SWE-bench (Jimenez
et al., 2024)) and end-to-end command-line tasks
(Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026)); assistants
by tool-use suites such as GAIA (Mialon et al.,
2024) and τ-bench (Yao et al., 2025). Machine-
learning and data-science agents are measured on
Kaggle-style pipelines (Chan et al., 2025; Starace
et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024;
Gu et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024).
These capture tool use and long-horizon execution
in a container—the harness we build on—but score
a leaderboard position or a rubric over a deliverable,
never a modeling artifact, and attach no feasibility
contract.
Mathematical
and
optimization
reasoning.
Closed-form mathematics benchmarks measure de-
duction, not modeling (Hendrycks et al., 2021;
Cobbe et al., 2021; Glazer et al., 2024; Zheng et al.,
2022). Operations-research systems parse word
problems into solver-ready formulations and eval-
uate optimality or feasibility of a given formula-
tion (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2024;
AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025;
Huang et al., 2025a; Mostajabdaveh et al., 2025;
Lima et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025). They supply
a strong execution-validity precedent—a solver cer-
tifies a solution is feasible or optimal for a stated

Mathematical-modeling
benchmarks
and
agents.
The closest work forms a continuum,
and none of it is simultaneously agentic, verifiable,
and terminal.
Mamo (Huang et al., 2025b) is
solver-grounded: models emit solver-consumable
artifacts and the solver is a falsifiable checker, giv-
ing a precise but narrow signal on formal fragments
rather than whole contest problems. ModelingA-
gent and its ModelingBench (Qian et al., 2025)
are report-level: open-ended problems graded by
an expert-style LLM judge—ecologically rich but
judge-calibration dependent and non-reproducible.
MM-Agent and MM-Bench (Liu et al., 2025) add
a hierarchical modeling library, yet their primary
evaluation remains a report rubric. TB-MathModel
keeps the full contest statement and the agentic
workflow, pins evaluation to a structured artifact
scored by an executable verifier, and adds a
feasibility layer neither camp provides.
Verification in evaluation.
Theorem provers
such as Lean 4 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) with
Mathlib (The mathlib Community, 2020) have
certified competition and research mathematics,
and RL over formal proof has produced strong
provers (Hubert et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2024). Us-
ing a prover not to find answers but to audit a
benchmark’s own feasibility decisions is, to our
knowledge, new: our Lean layer re-proves the pro-
grammatic gate’s invariants, so an assertion be-
comes a machine-checkable fact (Sutton, 2001),
at integer-and-rational arithmetic cost the kernel
decides without the full library.
Multimodal agents and reproduction-anchored
scoring.
Tool-using agents increasingly external-
ize their state for reuse (Yao et al., 2023; Wei et al.,
2022; Schick et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026). TB-
3


--- Page 4 ---
MathModel makes visual evidence load-bearing—
figures are cropped from the official PDFs—so har-
nesses with and without an image channel can be
compared on identical tasks. Anchoring a numeri-
cal benchmark on a published solution is standard
practice; we show it creates three under-reported
hazards (direction asymmetry, degenerate scoring
bands, unpinned units) and give auditable rules and
tests for each.
3
The TB-MathModel Benchmark
TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical
Modeling Bench) turns each contest problem into a
self-contained terminal task. Figure 2 summarises
the construction pipeline. A build script assembles
the official contest material into four parts: (i) an
instruction file with the verbatim statement and its
figures; (ii) an agent container holding the mirrored
attachments and an output schema; (iii) a separate
verifier container holding the scoring panel and
an executable feasibility check; and (iv) an oracle
that reproduces the Outstanding-award (O-award)
paper. The agent is dropped into the terminal with
this material and must return a single structured
artifact. Everything downstream of the artifact—
scoring and feasibility—is machine-executable.
Task selection and sources.
TB-MathModel
comprises 18 tasks: the A, B, and C problems of
CUMCM and MCM for each of 2023–2025. We re-
strict to the last three years on purpose: older prob-
lems predate capable LLMs and were calibrated
to software-assistant graders, so their task mix and
review standard differ from the post-LLM regime,
and recent editions are harder and more discrimi-
nating. The two contests complement each other—
CUMCM is engineering/optimization-heavy and
Chinese, MCM is modeling-flavored and English—
and taking all three problems of each year cov-
ers the standard “A = physical/engineering, B =
data/optimization, C = data-science” split with-
out cherry-picking. Statements and attachments
are mirrored verbatim; a statement’s figures are
cropped from the official PDF (artwork plus its
caption) and delivered inline and at stable con-
tainer paths. 21 unique figures across 6 tasks are
load-bearing: the statements reference them for ge-
ometry not restated in text (e.g., the dragon-dance
U-turn curve, which fixes the final head speed),
so a harness without an image channel cannot re-
cover it—hence the multimodal evaluation. TB-
MathModel is a pure evaluation set, with no train-
ing split or difficulty tiering (Appendix A).
The artifact contract and oracle anchors.
The
scored object is one JSON file per task, whose
schema (field names and types only) is shipped to
the agent; extra CSV/XLSX/PNG artifacts are not
scored. A schema-constrained JSON is what makes
an automated score possible, at the cost of mapping
a free-form effort onto named numeric fields—a
tension we revisit in Section 4.3. Each task is an-
chored to one O-award paper, re-implemented as a
script that reads the attachments and emits the same
JSON; the reproduction is the normalisation end-
point (O-EVAL = 100%) and sets the per-metric
panel, coverage 18/18. Provenance is a first-class
field—paper id, PDF/OCR source, and reproduc-
tion scope—so any anchor can be re-derived (Ap-
pendix D); this is what let us catch and correct an
infeasible dragon-dance anchor before it reached
the board.
3.1
Scoring: direction-aware, one-sided,
auditable
A naive distance-to-anchor metric silently re-
wards copying and punishes improvement, so
TB-MathModel scores each task through a per-
metric panel with an explicit semantic direc-
tion.
Each task ships a panel of 2–6 scored
metrics (60 in total), each with a path into
the artifact, an anchor value O, a direction,
and a weight.
A metric is higher_is_better,
lower_is_better, target_value (closest to O
wins), or exact_value, set from the modeling se-
mantics of the quantity rather than the sign of its
value. Directional metrics use an asymmetric, one-
sided reward: meeting or beating the anchor never
scores below 1.0, so improving on the paper is
never punished (full formulas in Appendix G).
Three failure modes recur often enough to de-
serve named rules. (i) Degenerate bands: a band
narrower than 2% of the value magnitude cannot
discriminate, so we widen it to 5%—this changed
one cell (stair-wear, 72.67 →73.52). (ii) Non-
comparable units: when an anchor is an arbi-
trary raw index with no schema-pinned unit (a host-
fish index of 1080), a model reporting the same
quantity normalised to [0, 1] is not wrong, so such
metrics are dropped for every model and the ora-
cle by a configuration-only rule. (iii) Cardinality
mismatch: surplus items are excluded rather than
counted missing. Out-of-domain values (a correla-
tion outside [−1, 1], a negative count) score zero,

Figure 2: The TB-MathModel construction and evaluation pipeline. Build: official statements, attachments, and
PDF figures are compiled into a task directory. Run: the agent works inside a network-isolated terminal container
and writes one JSON artifact. Evaluate: the artifact is scored by a direction-aware, one-sided panel against an
O-award reproduction, and independently checked by a programmatic feasibility gate plus a Lean 4 certificate layer;
a failed gate zeroes the task.
with the reason recorded.
Let R, F, O be the weighted panel raw of
a submission, of the DeepSeek V4 Flash base-
line, and of the oracle.
We report O-EVAL =
clamp(R/O, 0, 1) averaged over tasks (the head-
line absolute score) and a gap-compensated RO-
BUST BO-EVAL = clip((R −F)/(O −F), ±1)
when the oracle–baseline gap exceeds 0.10, and
the clipped raw gain R −F otherwise, with
ROBUST BO-EVAL = −1 for a missing artifact
(full formulas in Appendix G). Two properties are
locked by contract tests: oracle self-consistency
(every reproduction scores exactly 1.0) and one-
sidedness (at or above the anchor is never a failure).
A failed feasibility gate sets a task’s O-EVAL to 0
and ROBUST BO-EVAL to −1.
3.2
Multi-references evaluation
Modeling has no single correct answer, so a bench-
mark that normalises against one paper silently
converts one team’s choices into ground truth. TB-
MathModel instead asks every human expert. For
each task we extracted the final-question values
reported by all available Outstanding-award pa-
pers for that problem, giving 99 panel papers, 94
of which yield the scored quantity. Coverage
is 18/18 tasks and all available outstanding pa-
pers are used—1 to 18 per task (median 4), since
the number of O-award reports differs by problem.
Each paper is one vote.
Let M(t) be the scored metrics of task t, P(t)
its paper panel, and Sp ⊆M(t) the fields pa-
per p actually reports. Writing R(m, S) for the
weighted panel score of submission m restricted to
S (weights renormalised over S), the task score is
the panel mean
O-EVAL(m, t) =
1
|P̸=(t)|
X
p∈P̸=(t)
R(m, Sp),
(1)
where P̸=(t) = {p ∈P(t) : Sp̸ = ∅}. Each
paper thus contributes exactly “how close is the
model to this human answer, on the fields that hu-
man reported”. Because R(p, Sp) = 1, every paper
agrees with itself and the reproduction reproduces
the panel. Equal weighting keeps one human so-
lution to one vote, and a paper that reports only
a single field acts as a single-field check rather
than being discarded—the honest treatment of an
incomplete report.
A paper is never silently dropped.
When it
cannot supply the scored quantity it carries a
machine-readable exclusion_reason, of which
five forms occur:
number_only_in_figure,
5


--- Page 6 ---
figure_only,
figure_only_logistic_prior,
no_numeric_estimate,
and
different_unit_of_analysis;
these account
for the 5 of 99 papers outside the panel. Values are
never interpolated or adjusted toward the existing
anchor, and a paper’s different-but-equivalent unit
is converted explicitly and noted. Where a panel is
empty—possible when an MCM answer is prose
or figure only—the task falls back to the single
reproduced anchor, and a missing artifact scores 0,
so the denominator is always the fixed 18 tasks.
A panel also makes disagreement between hu-
mans visible instead of hiding it behind one an-
chor. On mcm-2024-c-tennis-momentum, 10 of
11 outstanding papers conclude that momentum
is supported while the reproduced anchor—itself
an O-award report—concludes it is not; on that
task a model scores 0.909 if it answers with the
majority and 0.091 if it matches the anchor, so the
score reflects which valid statistical test the model
chose rather than modeling quality. We mark such
literature-split tasks explicitly and exclude them
from any headline ranking, while keeping them
in the panel: they are the clearest evidence that a
single-anchor score would have been arbitrary.
Relative to the single-anchor board, this changes
ROBUST BO-EVAL into a multi-reference gain in-
dex against the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash baseline, an-
chored at 1.0:
MULTI-BO = 1 + clip
Ot −ft
1 −ft
, −1, +1

,
(2)
with ft the Flash score on task t and Ot the model’s,
averaged over tasks; when the remaining headroom
1 −ft is below 0.10 we fall back to 1 + clip(Ot −
ft, ±0.10), and a missing artifact scores −1. A
value of 1.0 therefore means “level with Flash”,
1.08 means “closed 8% of the remaining gap to the
human panel”; it is a ratio, not a percentage, and is
not comparable to O-EVAL.
3.3
Feasibility verification: two layers
Proximity to an anchor does not imply that an an-
swer is physically admissible: a submission can
match a reference value on one field while violat-
ing a stated constraint on another. TB-MathModel
verifies feasibility independently of scoring, in two
layers with different trust bases.
Layer 1: a programmatic gate over six decid-
able forms.
Every task registers one feasibility
check, and the registry covers 18/18 tasks; every
hard-error branch falls into one of six decidable
forms (Appendix Table 12). Checks are either struc-
tural/domain bounds (rates, correlations, probabil-
ities, non-negative counts, distributions summing
to 100, peak ≥average) or constraint replay (helio-
stat rated power ≥60 MW and installation height
∈[2, 6] m, dragon-dance head speed × amplifi-
cation ratio ≤2 m/s, a demand-capped revenue
ceiling, a union duration ≤the sum of its parts).
Three contracts keep the gate honest: coverage (a
task cannot ship ungated), oracle self-consistency
(the O-award reference must pass its own check),
and discrimination (synthetic and real-field vio-
lations must be rejected, while an empty artifact
warns rather than hard-fails). Four constraints that
need an independent replay rather than a field check
are recorded as whole-task penalties (Appendix G).
Layer 2: Lean certificates.
To make the gate’s
own correctness checkable, Layer 2 re-proves the
same invariants as Lean 4 theorems, so the au-
dit rests on the kernel. It generates 624 obliga-
tions across all 18 tasks, discharged by decide or
omega. No Mathlib is used—the propositions are
decidable on exact integers—and values are scaled
to integers, so there is no floating-point tolerance;
the one exception, a composite index, is declared
in the predicate because the tolerance is itself part
of the audited assumption. A trust audit (#print
axioms) reports only [propext, Quot.sound] or
none, with no sorryAx and no native_decide
(grep-checked). A discrimination suite mutates
one numeric leaf at a time and requires the build to
fail and to cite the field; ten mutations across all
six forms are rejected. Two soft warnings become
proofs: a tourism acceptance index is refuted for
the unit convention, and a sustainability score fits
neither convention within a declared budget.
Verification scope.
The two layers decide every
feasibility question that a structured artifact can
settle without a model of the physics (Appendix
Table 13): unit/value ranges (A) and internal con-
sistency (B). Whether the reported value reflects
real physical truth (C)—does the field really pro-
duce 60 MW?—is a property of the world rather
than of the artifact, so TB-MathModel verifies it
where the problem admits an independent replay.
Within this scope the layers are exact: any obli-
gation whose evidence is absent is reported as a
witnessed gap rather than silently satisfied, so the
audit never overstates what it has proved.
6


--- Page 7 ---
4
Experiments
4.1
Setup
We evaluate seven multimodal model/harness en-
tries, whose harness can open the cropped figures.
Each entry is run with three seeds per task and
reported as a mean with standard deviation; where
a model was run at two reasoning tiers we keep the
higher-scoring variant. Every row is scored with
the same scorer and current anchors, so the board
shares one scoring definition (Appendix C).
The prompt is the task’s instruction file, passed
verbatim: the contest statement, the cited figures
inline, and a fixed “Required Benchmark Artifact”
block naming the output path (Appendix E). Tasks
run in Docker containers—python:3.12-slim
with a fixed scientific stack, internet disabled,
model traffic through a local retry proxy—so an
agent cannot fetch solutions or install packages
at run time; limits are 2 CPUs, 8 GB, no GPU,
and a 4-hour timeout (Appendix B). Each multi-
modal entry is run three times per task and reported
as a mean with standard deviation; the one well-
posed task, dragon-dance, is additionally probed
four times, where the answers agreed to machine
precision (std=4.6 × 10−16).
4.2
Main result: the multimodal board
Table 2 is the main result: the seven multimodal
entries on all 18 tasks, each a three-seed mean (±
std); the per-entry configuration is in Appendix
Table 7. O-EVAL is the primary metric: the multi-
reference score of Section 3.2, i.e. the mean over
the human paper panel of how close the model is
to each accepted answer. MULTI-BO is the sec-
ondary, relative index of that same score against
the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash baseline, fixed at 1.000
cell-by-cell: 1.08 means the model closed 8% of
Flash’s remaining gap to the panel, so it is read
against the baseline and is not a percentage. Five
findings stand out.
1. The newest flagships lead. GPT-6 Astra +
codex (64.58 ± 2.93) and Fable 5.1 + claude-
code (63.11 ± 1.33) top the board, about 4.8
and 3.4 points above GPT-5.5 xhigh + codex
(59.75 ± 1.55), and both clear the Flash base-
line by 13.2% and 8.1% of the remaining gap
respectively.
2. Cost buys a real but bounded gap.
The
two leaders cost $246–$273 per run, while the
cheapest strong entry, DeepSeek-Flash + open-
code, reaches 59.81±1.25 at $2.54—about 4.8
points behind the leader at roughly 1/100 the
cost.
3. Cheap open models cluster below the flag-
ships. Among the low-cost entries DeepSeek-
Flash (59.81), Kimi K3 (58.23), GLM-5.3
(57.78), and Qwen3.8 Flash (52.66) span about
7 points, and only the two flagships exceed the
baseline index (1.132 and 1.081); DeepSeek-
Flash defines it at 1.000 and every other entry
falls below.
4. A small gap is not yet a resolved ranking. Per-
seed deviations reach 2.93 pp, so the ∼1.5 pp
separation between the two leaders and be-
tween GPT-5.5 and Flash sits inside one stan-
dard deviation; we report the order but do not
claim a significant difference between adjacent
rows.
5. More inference compute is not monotone.
Running DeepSeek-Flash at its maximum rea-
soning tier drops its multi-reference score to
48.11% and its MULTI-BO to 0.864, well be-
low the default tier’s 59.81 and 1.000, at higher
cost: a larger deliberative budget does not sim-
ply buy accuracy on these tasks.
Hard gate and cost.
The gate removes exactly
the cells whose answers violate a stated constraint
and leaves the ranking otherwise stable, so it is
surgical rather than a blanket penalty. Cost is dom-
inated by per-token price, not usage: GPT-5.5’s
$99.37 is mostly cache-read input and output at
roughly 33×/50× DeepSeek V4.1 Flash’s rates,
despite comparable token counts.
Harness sensitivity.
Each model is driven by an
agent harness, so a natural question is whether the
score reflects the model or the harness. Table 3
holds the model fixed and varies the harness, using
DeepSeek-Flash and four harnesses. The score is
essentially invariant: O-EVAL moves only 0.07 pp
across all four (59.81–59.88), far inside the per-
seed deviation, and the relative index moves in the
same narrow band. A model’s own harness fits
it marginally better—DeepSeek’s native harness
gives the highest O-EVAL (59.88) and MULTI-BO
(1.092)—but the difference is small. The board
therefore measures the model far more than the
harness it is wrapped in.

4.3
Analysis
Per-task O-EVAL for four representative entries is
in Appendix Table 6. Three patterns stand out. (a)
The CUMCM–MCM gap is large and model-
dependent. For the weaker entries, CUMCM cells
sit near 100% while MCM cells sit between 0%
and 60%: the engineering problems have well-
defined final numbers most models reach, whereas
MCM problems are more open and their anchors
more contestable. The strongest entries narrow
the gap only slightly (GPT-6 82.9 on CUMCM vs.
46.2 on MCM; GPT-5.5 79.7 vs. 39.8). A size-
able share of tasks is now solved near-perfectly—
expected of a current benchmark—and the board’s
discrimination comes from the open-ended MCM
problems.
(b) Two tasks are all-or-nothing.
On mcm-2024-b-submersible every entry scores
100%, while on mcm-2024-c-tennis even the flag-
ships score below 40%. Such tasks either fall inside
or outside the panel’s tolerance entirely, so they sep-
arate regimes of models but not models within one.
(c) Many low scores reflect reference scale/scope,
not modeling error. Several tasks contain a metric
whose model/panel ratio exceeds 5×: a host-fish
index reported near 1080 by some papers while
models give a normalised [0, 1] quantity; a sustain-
ability score near 1.007 against models reporting
a 0–100 utility; a 6 × 6 grid against models dis-
cretising the same region into hundreds of cells;
and a 72.67 →73.52 band in which the paper’s
own baseline scores zero.
Scoring pitfalls we found and fixed.
An anchor-
based benchmark is only as credible as its anchors,
so we audited every scoring rule and anchor and
report what the audit changed (Appendix G). Two
gate false positives were removed without mov-
ing any score, and degenerate-band widening af-
fected one cell (+0.35 pp). Excluding two non-
comparable-unit metrics raised every entry by 0.05–
8


--- Page 9 ---
2.62 pp—the signature of a systematic scoring ef-
fect rather than a model difference. Most conse-
quentially, the audit flagged the dragon-dance an-
chor as physically infeasible and we corrected it
(Section 4.2).
What the feasibility layers caught.
The gate
hard-invalidated 7 cells, concentrated on heliostat
(rated power below 60 MW, or a mirror below the
2 m minimum) plus single cells for smoke-screen,
Juneau, and Olympic. The Lean layer turns two
soft warnings into proofs and proves non-vacuity
by accepting a corrected artifact under the predicate
that rejects the reported one. On the one numer-
ically well-posed task the runs agree to machine
precision, and across the board the per-seed de-
viations stay small relative to the spread between
entries (Table 2), so rankings do not depend on the
seed.
4.4
From Findings to Model Development
TB-MathModel is meant to improve models, not
only rank them. Three levers follow from the find-
ings above, and each is trainable with signals TB-
MathModel already produces.
Verified reward for RL. The feasible, oracle-
normalised score is an executable, reproducible
reward—every submission passes the gate and the
Lean layer. Rejection-sampling (keep and rank
gate-accepted trajectories by O-EVAL) works to-
day; group-relative policy optimisation with the
gate as a hard multiplier teaches the model to sat-
isfy the physics before chasing the reference. The
dragon-dance case motivates this: twelve models
computed the right peak but were penalised, so
what they lack is self-checking—exactly what a
verifier in the reward provides.
Targets against the observed failures. Finding
(a)—the open-ended MCM suite separates qual-
ity while CUMCM saturates—says to train as-
sumptions, formulation, and sensitivity rather than
closed-form solving; finding (c)—many losses are
unit and scale mismatches—says to state and verify
units, ranges, and schema before emitting a number.
Both are rewarded directly by the artifact contract.
Feasibility the artifact can check. The dragon-
dance audit exposes the failure a value-range check
cannot: a consistent answer that is physically in-
admissible because the artifact omits the evidence
(no per-mirror layout, no peak-neighbourhood sam-
ple). Training models to emit that witness raises the
score and makes them checkable, reaching level C.
Case studies.
Three roles—a top proprietary
agent, the oracle, and the low-cost open agent—are
compared on three problems in Appendix F. On
dragon-dance all three converge while the paper’s
value is the infeasible outlier, so the models were
right and our anchor was wrong. On crop-planting
the paper’s constraints are jointly infeasible, so we
anchor on a reproducible exact MILP optimum. On
Juneau the sustainability score is reported on dif-
ferent unit scales, which is why the task schema,
not the scorer, must pin a field’s range.
5
Conclusion
We presented TB-MathModel, the first agentic
and verifiable terminal benchmark of 18 real
mathematical-modeling problems, distinguished by
direction-aware, one-sided scoring that never pe-
nalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility
verification combining a gate over six decidable
invariant forms with 624 kernel-checked Lean obli-
gations.
Scoring each task against a panel of human out-
standing papers, the newest flagships lead across
seven multimodal entries (GPT-6 Astra at O-EVAL
64.58%, Fable 5.1 at 63.11%), while the $2.54
open DeepSeek-Flash holds 59.81% at 1/100 the
cost. We documented the scoring pitfalls we fixed,
and showed a case where the benchmark itself was
wrong and the models were right.
The two-layer design is the transferable idea:
a fast gate covers every task and a proof assis-
tant makes the audit’s own correctness machine-
checkable, while stating what neither can answer.
Because TB-MathModel gives a reproducible re-
ward, its trajectories are also training material, and
Section 4.4 turns the findings into directions.
Acknowledgements
We thank OpenRefinery (https://openrefinery.
ai/) for providing the LLM API access and eval-
uation support that enabled our experiments with
GPT-6-Astra and Claude-Fable-5.1. In particular,
we thank Kai Du and Ding Fan of OpenRefinery
for their assistance. Their infrastructure and sup-
port were instrumental in conducting the model
evaluations reported in this paper. Any opinions,
findings, and conclusions expressed here are those
of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the
views of OpenRefinery.
9


--- Page 10 ---
Limitations
TB-MathModel normalises each task against a re-
producible Outstanding-award solution, with per-
anchor provenance so any reference can be re-
derived; because modeling admits no single cor-
rect answer, the natural extension is a multi-paper
panel reporting a spread over accepted solutions.
The two verification layers decide every feasibility
question a structured artifact can settle (unit/value
ranges and internal consistency); external physical
truth is a property of the world, so it is checked
where a problem admits an independent replay, and
any obligation whose evidence is missing is re-
ported rather than silently passed. Panel size varies
with the number of outstanding reports per prob-
lem (1 to 18 papers), and where humans themselves
disagree—as on the tennis momentum test, where
10 of 11 papers reach the opposite conclusion from
the anchor—we mark the task literature-split and
keep it out of headline rankings. Scores are three-
seed means, and the task shell carries over to engi-
neering and cross-disciplinary problems.
Ethical Considerations
Statements, attachments, and figures are official
CUMCM and MCM material used for research
evaluation; we do not redistribute Outstanding-
award solutions, and reproduction code derives
from a public corpus with per-task provenance.
Users should confirm the licence terms for their
own redistribution. TB-MathModel measures and
improves the modeling workflow of LLM agents
rather than automating work presented as a team’s
own, and entirely automated evaluation keeps the
cost of broad participation low.
Use of Large Language Models
LLMs served as the systems under test—every en-
try in Table 2 is an LLM agent, which is the object
of measurement—and as writing assistants that
helped draft prose and check the internal consis-
tency of LATEX and numbers. Benchmark construc-
tion, scoring rules, feasibility checks, and Lean
obligations were specified, implemented, and ver-
ified by the authors, and all numerical results are
produced by the released scripts.

Appendix Overview
This supplementary material makes the main pa-
per’s construction and claims auditable.
Ap-
pendix A gives the dataset composition, the per-
task table, the delivered directory structure, and
an explicit statement that TB-MathModel has no
train/validation/test split. Appendix B records the
software and hardware environment and the net-
work isolation policy. Appendix C lists the per-
entry configuration, the agent command templates,
and the retry/artifact-recovery details. Appendix D
disambiguates the three objects called “baseline”.
Appendix E reproduces the prompt template and
the harness-wrapping layer. Appendix F gives the
full numerics behind the three case studies. Ap-
pendix G gives the scoring formulas, the excluded
metrics, and the hard-gate decisions. Appendix H
catalogues the Lean obligations, the trust audit, and
the discrimination suite.
• Appendix A: dataset composition, per-task ta-
ble, delivered structure, and split
• Appendix B: host, agent container, verifier con-
tainer, resource limits, network isolation
• Appendix C: per-entry configuration, command
templates, retries, cost accounting
• Appendix D: flash baseline, Outstanding an-
chor, legacy endpoints, anchor caveats
• Appendix E: prompt structure, artifact block,
harness wrapping, version caveat
• Appendix F: full numeric case-study tables
• Appendix G: metric panel, formulas, excluded
metrics, hard gates
• Appendix H: obligation counts, representative
obligations, trust audit, discrimination suite
A
Dataset Details
A.1
Composition
TB-MathModel has 18 tasks, listed in Table 4
(main text). The composition is CUMCM (Chi-
nese) 2023, 2024, 2025 × problems A, B, C = 9
tasks, plus MCM (English) 2023, 2024, 2025 ×
problems A, B, C = 9 tasks. Each task is a full
contest problem with several sub-questions; only
the numeric core of the final question is scored.
Problem A is typically physical/engineering, B op-
timization/data, and C data-science, so taking all
three of each year avoids topical cherry-picking.
Figure 4: An official statement figure, cropped from
the CUMCM 2023 A PDF and delivered inline in the
prompt. 21 such figures across 6 tasks are load-bearing:
the final answer depends on reading them.
A.2
Per-task summary
Table 5 summarises each task. “#Fig.” counts
unique figures cropped from the official PDF;
“#Metric” is the number of scored metrics.
†60 scored metrics across the 18 tasks; one fur-
ther Wordle metric is declared at weight 0 and
excluded from scoring. The counts are verified
against the released tasks; the 21 figures are unique
after de-duplication and are delivered twice—once
inline in the instruction file and once under the
container figure path. Data sources are the offi-
cial contest material: CUMCM statements under
cumcm/problems/{year}/{X}.md and MCM un-
der mcm/problems/{year}/{X}.md; Outstanding-
paper PDFs/OCR used for anchors come from the
same corpus’s outstanding/ tree, and every task
records its paper identifier, the PDF/OCR source
paths, and its reproduction_scope.
A.3
Per-task multi-reference scores
A.4
Delivered structure
Each task directory contains an instruction file (the
prompt), a metadata file (limits), an environment
directory (agent image plus data), a tests directory
(verifier, scoring config, anchor), and a solution
directory (oracle). Inside the environment data
directory are the statement copy, the output schema
(field names and types only), a source manifest
mapping each visible file to its corpus path, the
verbatim attachments under flat filenames with an
index, a full-path mirror of the original corpus, and
the cropped figures for the six tasks that have them.
13


--- Page 14 ---
Table 4: The 18 TB-MathModel tasks and their O-award anchors. “Final Q” is the contest question whose numeric
core is scored; oracle coverage is 18/18.
Slug
Contest
Topic
Final Q
cumcm-2023-a-heliostat
CUMCM 2023 A

A.5
Split
There is no train/validation/test split.
TB-
MathModel is a pure evaluation set: the 18 tasks
are all evaluation tasks, evaluated uniformly, with
no held-out partition and no per-task difficulty
tier. (One task’s oracle model contains an in-task
train/test split for the Wordle problem; that is part
of that problem’s modeling content and is unrelated
to benchmark partitioning.)
B
Software and Hardware Environment
B.1
Host and framework
The evaluation harness runs from a macOS host
(arm64). It orchestrates per-task Docker containers;
the enforced resource limits are container limits,
not host limits.
B.2
Agent container
All 18 tasks use the same base and dependency
set. The base image is python:3.12-slim plus
uv. The Python environment at /opt/venv pins
NumPy 2.0.2, pandas 2.2.2, SciPy 1.14.1, scikit-
learn 1.5.2, Matplotlib 3.9.2 (MPLBACKEND=Agg),
openpyxl 3.1.5, and xlrd 2.0.1. Writable paths are
/root/data (read-only inputs), /root/results
(the scored artifact), and /logs/agent.
B.3
Verifier container
The verifier runs in a separate container built from
a minimal python:3.12-slim image installing
only pytest. It has no network and no access
to the agent’s working directory beyond the copied
artifacts. The verifier timeout is 180 s.
B.4
Resource limits
The limits are identical for all tasks: 2 CPUs,
8192 MB memory, 20480 MB storage, 0 GPUs.
The build timeout is 900 s and the agent timeout
14400 s (4 h), also stated at the end of each prompt.
The recorded runs used one concurrent trial and no
retries.
B.5
Network isolation
Every task disables internet access. Model traf-
fic is routed through a local retry proxy, so an
agent can call the model API but cannot fetch so-
lutions, download packages, or install tooling at
run time. Because installation is impossible af-
ter a trial starts, CLI agents (codex, opencode,
claude-code) must be present in the image; the
third-party operator’s runs pre-installed the CLIs
at the end of the Dockerfile and allow-listed only
the model gateway, leaving the statement, data, and
verifier unchanged.
B.6
Frozen versions
For reproducibility we pin the harness version, the
Python dependency set above, and the local pricing
snapshot used for cost, so that the reported costs
are stable across reruns.

C
Experimental Settings
C.1
Per-entry configuration and results
Table 7 lists the seven multimodal entries with the
harness and reasoning tier actually passed and their
full scores. Multimodal status means the harness
exposes an image channel. Every entry is run with
three seeds per task.
C.2
Agent command templates
The task statement is passed to the agent as
its prompt. Representative commands from the
recorded trials:
# codex
codex exec --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --skip-
git-repo-check \
--model gpt-5.5 --json --enable unified_exec \
-c model_reasoning_effort=xhigh -- '<instruction.md body>'
# opencode
opencode --model=openai/deepseek-flash run --format=json --
thinking \
--dangerously-skip-permissions -- '<instruction.md body>'
Each CLI harness receives the statement as its posi-
tional prompt; the harness prepends its own generic
system prompt before it.
C.3
Retries, concurrency, and artifact
recovery
All entries used one concurrent trial and no au-
tomatic retries; each of the three seeds is an in-
dependent pass over the 18 tasks. Two subtleties
are disclosed. First, misfiled artifacts: two tasks
wrote the result with a hyphen instead of the re-
quired underscore, so the harness did not collect it;
we replayed the recorded run’s scripts to reproduce
the artifact and re-scored it. Second, third-party
runs: the GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 entries were
run by independent operators; because their veri-
fier used a different reward formula, we re-scored
their saved artifacts with our scorer and current
anchors so that all entries share one scoring def-
inition. Where an artifact was not packaged, we
reconstructed the scored fields from the saved per-
metric records, verified to reproduce the operator’s
own numbers exactly on the tasks where the full
artifact was present.
C.4
Cost accounting
Cost is computed from measured token usage
against a fixed price snapshot, with two conser-
vative adjustments stated in the report: reasoning
tokens that a provider bills outside its completion
counter are added to output, and where a provider
charges a peak/off-peak rate, the peak rate is used.
For the two third-party entries, cost is their own
measured per-run USD. Because the pricing file is
local and fixed, costs do not drift between reruns.
D
Baseline Information
The word “baseline” is overloaded in this bench-
mark; we distinguish three distinct objects so that
the numbers are unambiguous.
D.1
The flash baseline (score normalisation)
ROBUST BO-EVAL is computed against a single
reference submission, the DeepSeek V4 Flash base-
line run on the same tasks. It defines the zero point:

ROBUST BO-EVAL normalises the model–baseline
gain by the oracle–baseline gap. It is a model sub-
mission, not a curated baseline panel.
D.2
The Outstanding anchor (score ceiling)
Each task’s ceiling is the reproduction of one
Outstanding-award paper, which is the value that
scores O-EVAL= 100%. Table 8 lists the anchor
paper identifier for each task. Each anchor is a
runnable script that reads the official attachments
and emits the artifact JSON, plus a committed
expected result recording its values; coverage is
18/18.
D.3
Legacy per-task baseline endpoints
Fifteen of the 18 tasks use the legacy target-
distance-to-Outstanding
mode
with
a
base-
line endpoint; three (Wordle, stair-wear, and
Juneau tourism) use true per-metric baseline-to-
Outstanding min–max endpoints. The distinction
is recorded per metric in each scoring configuration
and surfaced in the per-task tables.
D.4
Anchor caveats
Two anchors carry caveats that affect how their
scores should be read. Crop-planting is a marked
special case: the paper’s full constraint set is
jointly infeasible on the official attachments and
its reported value came from an undisclosed
heuristic, so the anchor is a reproducible exact
MILP optimum under the paper’s per-plot demand
cap. Dragon-dance was corrected: the paper’s
1.406276 m/s is infeasible (a handle would reach
2.2568 m/s), so the anchor is the continuous-time
value 1.246266 m/s and the metric direction is
target_value. Both are examples of the general
principle that an anchor is a reproduction of one
team’s choices, and that its provenance must be
inspectable.

E
Prompt Design
E.1
The prompt is the task statement
There is no hand-written prompt wrapper in this
benchmark. The prompt is the task’s instruction
file, delivered verbatim by the harness. Its structure
is fixed across tasks: a machine-readable canary
comment (stripped before delivery); an “Original
Contest Problem” section containing the verbatim
statement with each cited figure embedded inline;
any results tables the statement requires, as plain
text; a note listing the in-container figure paths;
a “Required Benchmark Artifact” section; and the
time-limit line.
E.2
The artifact block (verbatim template)
# Required Benchmark Artifact
Solve the contest problem above. The official attachments are
mirrored at
`/root/data/attachments` (flat filenames; see
`/root/data/attachments/INDEX.md`) and also remain at their
full corpus paths
under `/root/data/repo`. Use them whenever they are relevant.
Write your final
structured answer to:
/root/results/<slug>_result.json
The result must be valid JSON and should follow the shape
shown in
`/root/data/output_schema.json`. Include the numerical
quantities, modeling
decisions, diagnostics, sensitivity or uncertainty results,
conclusions for the
contest questions, and generated artifact paths needed to
support your answer.
You may also write supplementary CSV, XLSX, or PNG files under
`/root/results`,
but the JSON file above is the required artifact.
You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by
using online
solutions or hints specific to this task.
E.3
Harness wrapping
The harnesses deliver the same text differently.
Each CLI harness prepends its own generic
command-line system prompt and then supplies
the statement as the positional prompt.
E.4
Version caveat
The instruction files were revised after some trials
were recorded: a figure-path section was added,
and one MCM statement was re-sourced from the
official PDF. The prompt actually delivered in a
given trial is the one captured in that trial’s log;
for reproducibility, cite those, not the current file.
This is why we describe the prompt structure above
rather than quoting today’s file as if it were what
every model saw.
E.5
What the prompt withholds by design
By design the prompt is a pure task description:
no modeling hints, no method suggestions, and no
pointer to the scored fields beyond the schema. It
leaves the agent to infer which numbers matter,
which keeps the setting a test of the whole model-
ing problem rather than a fill-in-the-schema exer-
cise. This keeps the benchmark a test of doing the
whole modeling problem, at the cost of the agent
having to infer which numbers matter.
F
Case Studies (Full Numerics)
We give the full per-field comparison for the three
case studies. Values are read from each role’s saved
artifact; the oracle column is the anchor. All three
tables span both columns.
The reconstruction of the true peak is a
continuous-time maximum of the handle-speed ra-
tio; the paper sampled integer seconds and stepped
over it. The exact identity head_speed×ratio=
2 m/s, checked by both the programmatic gate and
the Lean layer, is what exposes the paper value as
infeasible: the paper’s isolated value 1.406276 m/s
(with ratio 1.422195) implies 2.2568 m/s at a han-
dle.
The paper’s full constraint set is infeasible on the
official attachments, so the anchor is a reproducible
MILP optimum and the models’ plans sit in the
same regime. The anchor lies between the two

This is the clearest scale problem. The anchor
is on a ∼1 unit scale; one third-party agent reports
the same field on a 0–100 “multiattribute utility”
scale that it explicitly declares in its own artifact.
Because the task’s output schema does not pin the
range, the agent is not wrong—which is why the
correct repair is to specify the field’s range in the
schema, not to rescale in the scorer.
F.1
Discussion
Dragon-dance.
The paper’s isolated value
(1.406276) is the wrong one. This case matters
most because it inverts the usual story: the models
were right and the reference was wrong, and the fix
was to the benchmark. It also shows why the feasi-
bility layer is not redundant with scoring—“ratio ×
head speed = 2 m/s” is an exact identity that both
layers check, and it is what made the paper value’s
infeasibility visible.
Crop-planting. GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek produce
plan profits in the same regime, and the optimum
sits between them on one column—which is why a
single scalar cannot summarise the task. When the
human paper is not reproducible, the honest move
is to anchor on a reproducible value and mark it, not
to penalise models for matching an irreproducible
number.
Juneau. The oracle recommends an 11,000/day
cap at 55 USD with a sustainability score of 1.007,
GPT-5.5 recommends 20,000/day at 20 USD on
its own 0–1 scale, and DeepSeek recommends
16,000/day at 30 USD. This argues that the task
schema—not just the scorer—must state a field’s
range and units, which is a fix to the task rather
than to the code.
G
Scoring Details
G.1
The metric panel
Every task ships a scoring configuration declaring
its scored metrics. A metric entry specifies a path
into the artifact, an oracle value, optional baseline
and outstanding values, a direction (with a match-
ing semantic direction), a normalisation mode, and
a weight. Across the 18 tasks there are 60 scored
metrics; one further Wordle metric is declared at
weight 0 and recorded but excluded from the panel.
The per-task counts are in Table 5.
G.2
Formulas
Let R be a submission’s weighted panel raw, F
the DeepSeek V4 Flash baseline’s, O the ora-
cle’s, and gap = O −F. We report O-EVAL =
clamp(R/O, 0, 1) and a gap-compensated RO-
BUST BO-EVAL based on the raw gain R −F:
clip

R−F
gap , ±1

if gap ≥0.10,
clip(R −F, ±0.10) otherwise,
where
±
denotes
the
symmetric
bound.
A
missing
or
non-scoreable
artifact
gets
ROBUST BO-EVAL
=
−1.
The per-metric
reward is given in Section 3.1; the one-sided
property (meeting or beating the anchor never
scores below 1.0) is locked by a contract test.
G.3
Excluded metrics
Two metrics are excluded from the panel for every
model and the oracle, both by configuration-only
rules: the Olympic fourth recommendation (the
prompt asks for three countries but the reproduc-
tion emits four rows), and the two lamprey raw
population indices when the anchor magnitude ex-
ceeds 5 (the anchor is an arbitrary raw index with
no schema-pinned unit). Out-of-domain values

Table 12: The six decidable invariant forms covering
the hard-error branches of all 18 tasks.
Form
Example obligation
domain / range
probability ∈[0, 1]; thickness > 0
integer / binary
decision bits ∈{0, 1}; counts integer
ordering
q95 ≥mean; peak ≥average
exact identity
area = count × w × h; union ≤P
finite domain
decision-bit count ∈{16, 17}
partition / sum
land-use counts sum to the grid
(correlations outside [−1, 1], unit-interval quanti-
ties outside [0, 1], negative counts, non-positive
physical quantities) are not excluded but have their
reward set to zero, with the reason recorded.
G.4
Hard-gate decisions
Seven whole-task penalties were applied across the
entries: four heliostat violations (rated power be-
low 60 MW, or a mirror below the 2 m minimum),
one smoke-screen plan failing an independent cov-
erage replay, one Juneau answer with unit-invalid
acceptance/sustainability values, and one Olympic
answer with a degenerate coach-effect result.
G.5
Pitfalls found and fixed
An anchor-based benchmark is only as credible as
its anchors, so we audited the scoring rules and
anchors and report what the audit changed. Two
gate false positives (a signed elasticity read as a
negative count; a missing field read as a hard con-
tradiction) were corrected but changed no score,
and degenerate-band widening moved one score
(+0.35 pp for v4 pro). Non-comparable-unit ex-
clusion raised every entry by 0.05–2.62 pp, since
the penalty applied to all submissions equally—
the signature of a systematic scoring error rather
than a model difference.
Finally, the dragon-
dance anchor was itself physically infeasible: the
paper’s 1.406276 m/s would drive a handle to
1.406276 × 1.604793 = 2.2568 m/s, above the
2 m/s cap, because it maximised over integer sec-
onds and stepped over the true continuous-time
peak at t = 14.48 s. We corrected the anchor to
1.246266 m/s; twelve of the evaluated models had
reported the correct value and had been sitting at
49.82%, while the two matching the erroneous pa-
per value had been at 100%. Here the benchmark,
not the model, was wrong (Appendices G and H).
G.6
Degenerate-band and validity rules
The band-widening rule applies to the endpoint
metrics of the three endpoint-style tasks. Apply-
ing all scoring fixes in this paper moved every en-
try upward by 0.05–2.62 pp, because the affected
penalties applied to all submissions equally—the
diagnostic signature of a systematic scoring error
rather than a model difference.
H
Lean Obligation Catalogue
H.1
Per-task obligation counts
The generator emits one obligation per checkable
field; the totals by task are in Table 14.
Four skipped obligations are visible in the gener-
ator output: one missing overlap field (multibeam),
scenarios whose declared grid count is null (Maasai
partition), and one recommendation-count interpre-
tation difference (Olympic).
H.2
Representative obligations
Over the invariant library, a task supplies bounds
and the obligations are generated. Examples:
-- domain/range: a rate must lie in [0,1] (scaled x1000)
example : (0 <= 43 /\ 43 <= 1000) := by decide
-- ordering: q95 must not fall below the mean
example : (posterior_mean <= posterior_q95) := by ...
-- exact identity: head_speed * ratio = 2 m/s (scaled)
example : (1980000 <= 1246266 * 1604793 /\ 1246266 * 1604793
<= 2020000) := by decide
-- finite domain: count of decision bits is 16 or 17
example : (len = 16 \/ len = 17) := by decide
Every generated obligation is annotated with the
JSON path it came from, so a reviewer can trace
each claim back to the artifact.

H.3
Trust audit (condensed excerpt)
'Feasibility.atMost_trans'
axioms: propext, Quot.sound
'Feasibility.atLeast_mono'
axioms: propext, Quot.sound
'CropPlanting.ua_feasible'
no axioms
'CropPlanting.ua_in_interpretation_gap'
no axioms
'Juneau.ua_acceptance_percent_only'
no axioms
'Juneau.ua_sustainability_out_for_any_sane_tol'
axioms: propext, Quot.sound
'JuneauSensitivity.reported_infeasible'
axioms: propext, Quot.sound
Only propext and Quot.sound (Lean’s standard
classical logic) appear, or no axioms at all. There is
no sorryAx and no Lean.ofReduceBool (i.e. no
native_decide); the pipeline greps for both.
H.4
Discrimination suite
The discrimination script mutates one numeric leaf
at a time and requires the build to fail and to cite
the mutated field. Ten mutations across the six
forms are covered (out-of-range probability, out-of-
range correlation, reversed ordering, violated exact
identity, non-positive thickness, reversed interval,
non-binary decision bit, negative acceptance index,
q95 below mean, zero species count). All ten are
rejected; the suite exits non-zero if any is not.
H.5
Reproducing the layer
Toolchain is Lean 4 via elan, with no Mathlib; a
clean build completes in about a second. The gen-
erator also runs against the committed Outstanding-
award references, so the layer can be exercised
without the saved agent artifacts.
